notes: 20 items: 3 lifted-style, 17 fresh. Identify London (dispersion), dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding interactions in given compounds from structure.

items.question: Name the THREE types of intermolecular forces (IMFs) covered in CAPS Physical Sciences.
items.expectedAnswer: London (dispersion), dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding.
items.explanation: London (in all molecules), dipole-dipole (polar molecules), hydrogen bonding (H attached to N/O/F).
options: London (dispersion), dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding.
Ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds.
London, dipole-dipole, and ionic bonding.

items.question: Identify the strongest intermolecular force present in liquid H₂O.
options: London
Dipole-dipole
Hydrogen bonding
Ionic
items.expectedAnswer: Hydrogen bonding
items.explanation: H is bonded to O (an N/O/F atom) ⇒ hydrogen bonding possible. H-bonding is the strongest of the three IMFs present in water.

items.question: What intermolecular forces are present in liquid CH₄ (methane)?
items.expectedAnswer: London (dispersion) forces only — CH₄ is non-polar.
items.explanation: Non-polar tetrahedral methane: London only.
options: London + dipole-dipole (CH₄ is polar).
London (dispersion) forces only — CH₄ is non-polar.
Hydrogen bonding (H bonded to C).

items.question: What intermolecular forces are present in liquid HCl?
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole (HCl is polar, but Cl doesn't allow H-bonding).
items.explanation: Polar molecules have London + dipole-dipole. H-bonding requires H on N/O/F — Cl doesn't qualify in CAPS.
options: London + dipole-dipole + hydrogen bonding.
London only (HCl is non-polar).
London + dipole-dipole (HCl is polar, but Cl doesn't allow H-bonding).

items.question: What intermolecular forces are present in liquid NH₃ (ammonia)?
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole + hydrogen bonding (N-H allows H-bonding).
items.explanation: Polar + H bonded to N ⇒ all three IMFs. H-bonding is the strongest.
options: London + dipole-dipole + hydrogen bonding (N-H allows H-bonding).
London + dipole-dipole only (no H-bonding).
London forces only.

items.question: A student says: 'All POLAR molecules have hydrogen bonding.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect — H-bonding also needs an H bonded directly to N, O, or F.
items.explanation: Polar ⇒ dipole-dipole. H-bonding requires the H-on-N/O/F structural feature in addition.
options: Correct — every polar molecule hydrogen-bonds.
Incorrect — H-bonding also needs an H bonded directly to N, O, or F.
Correct — polarity and hydrogen bonding are the same thing.

items.question: A student says: 'Non-polar molecules don't have any intermolecular forces.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect — all molecules have London (dispersion) forces.
items.explanation: London is in EVERY molecule. Non-polar molecules have only London (no dipole-dipole or H-bonding).
options: Correct — non-polar molecules have no intermolecular forces.
Correct — only polar molecules experience London forces.
Incorrect — all molecules have London (dispersion) forces.

items.question: Identify the IMFs present in each: (a) Cl₂; (b) H₂O; (c) CH₃OH; (d) CO₂.
items.expectedAnswer: Cl₂: London; H₂O: London+dipole+H-bond; CH₃OH: London+dipole+H-bond; CO₂: London only.
items.explanation: Check polarity (shape matters!) + check H on N/O/F. CO₂ is a classic non-polar despite polar bonds.
options: Cl₂: London; H₂O: London+dipole+H-bond; CH₃OH: London+dipole+H-bond; CO₂: London only.
Cl₂: dipole-dipole; H₂O: London only; CH₃OH: London only; CO₂: H-bonding.
All four have hydrogen bonding.

items.question: Which of the following CAN form hydrogen bonds with itself: CH₃OH, CH₃Br, CH₃F, CH₃NH₂, CH₃COOH?
items.expectedAnswer: CH₃OH, CH₃NH₂, and CH₃COOH (each has H bonded to O or N).
items.explanation: H-bond donor needs H bonded to N/O/F. Check each structure for such an H.
options: CH₃OH, CH₃F, and CH₃Br.
CH₃OH, CH₃NH₂, and CH₃COOH (each has H bonded to O or N).
All five can hydrogen bond with themselves.

items.question: Which intermolecular force is the WEAKEST in general?
options: London (dispersion)
Dipole-dipole
Hydrogen bonding
Ionic
items.expectedAnswer: London (dispersion)
items.explanation: Strength ranking: H-bonding > dipole-dipole > London (within similar molecular sizes). London is the weakest per pair of molecules, BUT for large non-polar molecules, total London can be larger than dipole-dipole on smaller polar molecules.

items.question: Why do LONDON forces increase in strength as the molecule grows larger?
items.expectedAnswer: Larger molecules have more electrons (more polarisable) and more surface contact.
items.explanation: More electrons + more surface contact ⇒ stronger London. Long alkanes can have very strong total London despite being non-polar.
options: Because larger molecules are more polar.
Because larger molecules have more hydrogen bonds.
Larger molecules have more electrons (more polarisable) and more surface contact.

items.question: Determine the IMFs in liquid CH₃CHO (ethanal/acetaldehyde).
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole (polar C=O, but no H on O ⇒ no H-bonding).
items.explanation: Aldehyde: polar (C=O dipole), but no H-on-O so no H-bonding.
options: London + dipole-dipole (polar C=O, but no H on O ⇒ no H-bonding).
London + dipole-dipole + hydrogen bonding.
London only (ethanal is non-polar).

items.question: Why does HF form unusually strong hydrogen bonds?
items.expectedAnswer: F is the most electronegative atom, so the H-F bond is very polar.
items.explanation: Strongest electronegativity difference + small atomic size of F ⇒ very strong H-bonds.
options: Because HF is a very large, heavy molecule.
F is the most electronegative atom, so the H-F bond is very polar.
Because fluorine has many lone pairs to share.

items.question: Identify the IMFs present between two molecules of CH₃OCH₃ (dimethyl ether).
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole (polar C-O-C, but no O-H ⇒ no H-bonding).
items.explanation: Ether: polar molecule, but no H-on-O ⇒ no self-H-bonding. London + dipole-dipole.
options: London + dipole-dipole + hydrogen bonding.
London only (the ether is non-polar).
London + dipole-dipole (polar C-O-C, but no O-H ⇒ no H-bonding).

items.question: A learner draws a hydrogen bond between two CH₃Cl molecules. Is this correct? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect — the H atoms are bonded to C, not to N/O/F, so no H-bonding.
items.explanation: H-on-Cl or H-on-C doesn't qualify for H-bonding in CAPS.
options: Incorrect — the H atoms are bonded to C, not to N/O/F, so no H-bonding.
Correct — CH₃Cl is polar, so it hydrogen bonds.
Correct — chlorine allows hydrogen bonding like F.

items.question: List the IMFs in propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH).
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole + hydrogen bonding (the -OH provides H on O).
items.explanation: Alcohol: -OH ⇒ H-bonding capable. All three IMFs present.
options: London + dipole-dipole only (no H-bonding).
London + dipole-dipole + hydrogen bonding (the -OH provides H on O).
London forces only.

items.question: Why does CO₂ (linear) have NO net dipole moment despite having polar C=O bonds?
items.expectedAnswer: CO₂ is linear, so its two C=O bond dipoles point opposite and cancel.
items.explanation: Symmetry can cancel bond dipoles. Linear CO₂: O=C=O bonds opposite ⇒ cancel.
options: Because the C=O bonds are actually non-polar.
Because CO₂ is a bent molecule.
CO₂ is linear, so its two C=O bond dipoles point opposite and cancel.

items.question: Which has STRONGER intermolecular forces: CH₃CH₂CH₃ (propane) or CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol)?
items.expectedAnswer: Ethanol — it has hydrogen bonding (the -OH), which propane lacks.
items.explanation: H-bonding dominates between molecules of similar size. Ethanol > propane in IMF strength.
options: Ethanol — it has hydrogen bonding (the -OH), which propane lacks.
Propane — it is a larger, heavier molecule.
Equal — both are similar-sized organic molecules.

items.question: True or False: 'A small polar molecule (like HCl) has stronger IMFs than a long non-polar molecule (like decane, C₁₀H₂₂).' Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: False — decane is much larger, so its many London forces exceed HCl's forces.
items.explanation: Size of London matters: cumulative London on a long chain can outweigh dipole-dipole on a small polar molecule.
options: True — polar molecules always have stronger IMFs than non-polar ones.
False — decane is much larger, so its many London forces exceed HCl's forces.
True — small molecules always have stronger forces.

items.question: Why does HF have a higher boiling point than HCl, despite Cl being heavier than F?
items.expectedAnswer: HF can hydrogen bond (H on F); HCl cannot, so HF boils higher despite Cl being heavier.
items.explanation: H-bonding in HF >> London + dipole-dipole in HCl. H-bonding wins despite HF being smaller.
options: Cl is heavier, so HCl should boil higher — the statement is wrong.
Because HCl is non-polar and HF is polar.
HF can hydrogen bond (H on F); HCl cannot, so HF boils higher despite Cl being heavier.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_LONDON_UNIVERSAL: Doesn't recognise London is present in all molecules
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_SHAPE_POLARITY: Misuses molecular shape to determine polarity
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_LONDON_SIZE_DEPENDENCE: Doesn't recognise London grows with molecular size
